title: Two Requisitions, Two Bands
description: The same job in the same city is advertised twice, a hundred and eighty thousand dollars apart. The question that has to be asked before any number is spoken, and what to say in each branch.

lines.text: Two adverts. Same company, same city, same work. The gap between their ceilings is a hundred and eighty thousand dollars.
That is more than the whole of the lower advert. It is a second salary sitting in the difference.
Then obviously you apply to the higher one. This is not a hard problem.
He applied to the lower one, on the eleventh of August, and the call on Thursday came from that application.
Then it is already lost.
It is not lost. It is one question, asked at the right minute, by the right person.
The wrong person to ask it is her. The right person is him, and the right minute is early.
This is The DeployCo Screen. This episode is about the six minutes near the end where money comes up.
The lazy version says never discuss salary in a first call. Deflect and deal with it later.
That advice assumes one band that you cannot see. Here there are two bands and both are published.
When the numbers are public there is no information to protect. Deflecting just leaves the default in place.
And the default is the advert he applied through, which tops out exactly at his floor.
So the goal is to name a higher number.
No. The goal is to change which advert the conversation is about, before any number is named at all.
Numbers argued inside the wrong requisition go nowhere, because the recruiter cannot pay above a band she does not own.
Three things to understand about how this works inside a company.
First, a recruiter cannot exceed a band. She can move you between requisitions. She cannot rewrite one.
So a salary conversation inside the wrong requisition is a negotiation nobody in the room can win.
Surely she would move him herself if he were obviously senior.
Sometimes. More often the application arrives filed against a requisition and stays there because nobody questioned it.
Second, the first number spoken becomes the reference point for everything after it.
If he says a hundred and seventy-five, every later conversation is an argument about how far above a hundred and seventy-five he can get.
If she says the band is a hundred and thirty-five to three hundred and sixty, the conversation starts somewhere else entirely.
Third, equity here is not an ordinary grant, because this is not an ordinary company.
DeployCo is a joint venture inside a reported ten billion dollar vehicle with nineteen investors.
Equity in a private subsidiary is a lottery ticket. Not worth spending call time on.
It might be a lottery ticket. Asking what instrument it is tells you whether they know, which is itself information.
Now the moment, played out. There are two branches and both are fine if you take them deliberately.
She will describe the role at some point in the first fifteen minutes. That is the opening.
You say: can I ask which requisition this is against, because I think there may be two.
Then the reason. I applied through the Tomoro advert, which publishes one thirty to one eighty.
Your own board has a Sydney forward deployed engineer role posted on the seventh of August at one thirty-five to three sixty.
And the body of that one describes a senior applied AI software engineer. Which am I being considered for?
That is a lot of detail to recite at a recruiter.
It is four sentences and every one of them is checkable on her own systems. That is why it works.
Branch one. She says it is the DeployCo forward deployed role. Good. Now you can talk about numbers.
Based on the scope in that advert, owning architecture across engagements, setting the evaluation approach, mentoring.
I'd be looking at two hundred to two forty base, and I'd want to understand the equity before fixing on a figure.
Branch two. She says it is the Tomoro requisition, at one thirty to one eighty.
Then you say it plainly. One eighty is my floor, so on that band I'd only be workable at the top of it.
I'd rather be considered against the forward deployed role. Can we do that?
And if she says no?
Then you have learned something real on day one instead of week four, and you have lost nothing.
Four numbers, said twice, because they have to be available without thinking.
One thirty to one eighty. The Tomoro advert, published September twenty twenty-five, never refreshed.
One thirty-five to three sixty plus equity. The DeployCo Sydney advert, published the seventh of August this year.
The midpoint of the wide band is about two hundred and forty-seven thousand.
Nobody gets the midpoint of a band that wide at four months of production experience.
Agreed, and he is not asking for it. He is asking for two hundred to two forty, which sits below the midpoint.
His floor is one hundred and eighty thousand. That number stays private and it never gets said out loud.
A floor spoken aloud stops being a floor and becomes the offer.
One thirty to one eighty. One thirty-five to three sixty. Two hundred to two forty as the ask.
And one date to have ready. The seventh of August, which is when the Sydney role went live.
The whole move in one pass, nothing new.
She describes the role. You ask which requisition, and you give the two bands as the reason for asking.
She answers. If it is the forward deployed role, you tie your range to the scope in that advert.
Two hundred to two forty, then a question about the equity instrument, and then you stop talking.
If it is the legacy requisition, you name your floor as a constraint and ask to be moved.
Either way, no number left your mouth before you knew which band it was landing in.
Three ways this goes wrong, each with an early signal.
First, answering the expectations question directly. She asks, you answer, and it is over in four seconds.
The early signal is the shape of her question. What are you looking for, salary-wise, is a request for an anchor.
Refusing to answer a direct question is rude, and recruiters hate it.
He is not refusing. He is asking one question first and then answering fully. That is not the same thing.
Second, quoting the range but sounding unsure. Two hundred to two forty, said as a question, becomes two hundred.
The early signal is your own voice going up at the end. Say the range flat, then stop.
Third, negotiating against yourself in the silence. She pauses, and you fill it by lowering the number.
The early signal is the silence itself. Recruiters use silence, and it is not disapproval.
After you name a range, the next person to speak should be her.
Three things, as questions to ask yourself in the call.
Have I asked which requisition, before a number left my mouth?
Am I quoting a range tied to the scope in their advert, rather than to what I earn now?
Have I asked what the equity actually is, given this is a joint venture and not a normal subsidiary?
And if the whole thing goes past without money coming up at all?
Then you raise the requisition question anyway, at the end, under what happens next.
Self-test. What is the first thing you say when she asks about salary expectations?
Not a number. A question about which requisition, with the two bands as the reason for asking.
Next time: the questions you ask her, and how to read the answers she gives.
